topics.title: Running a Training Program
topics.text:
This is a question about what direction one can take with coaching a group of rising HS freshman through a series of competitions, at around AMC 8-10 Level.



Currently, the team that I'm working with doesn't have a wealth of talent; there is only one student with so-called "innate" talent, but he has close to IMO-level potential, so I wouldn't include him in this group. When they took the AMC 8 as 8th graders, the average was around a 17, which shows that they are at a fairly elementary level. During the one year that I have to work with these students, I want to get them to around a 23, which was where I was at the beginning of my MS years.



There are a number of problems, however:

1. As a mostly self-taught student (through AoPS books and AMC 8/10/12 Problems), I don't see what direction I can take with a larger group of students.

2. We only have 1 session per week, and the only way I can get them to spend a lot of time on maths is to assign them homework.

3. The school that I go to has never held any "structured" form of competition math training, so it's virtually impossible for me to obtain any nugget of advice from the teachers.



So the key phrases are: "AMC 8 Level", "Not a lot of time", "Fortunately, lots of motivation to improve".



With this, what direction can I take? I personally insist on taking one of the two paths: 1. Lecture-style classes using an AoPS textbook. 2. Roundtable discussions where we tackle a number of AMC 8-10 Level questions together. (Both approaches will have sessions for fully-timed AMC 8 Practice Tests)



Personally, I'm much happier to go with 2, but I'm worried that they're not conceptually prepared for some questions. Please help suggest any potential approaches with this program - also, if you prefer the first approach, please recommend me some good books! (I've heard that the Middle School Competition Maths book was good, but these kids aren't in MS anymore, so...)



Thanks!

3) If Palau, a small island nation in the Pacific grew at the same rate as Sweden, what will its population be in $2021$? As of $2016$, it has a population of just $21,503$.



4) If Sierra Leone suffers the same population decline as Japan, what will its population be in $2021$? Its population is currently $7,396,000$.



5) Find the total population of Germany, France, UK, Indonesia, Nauru, Kenya, Ethiopia, Jamaica, and Cuba. Is it greater than the population of the USA? You have to search it up by yourself.

topics.title: Pls explain the proof of the theorem
topics.text:
Theorem  : let f(x) be a polynomial.let p q be integers without a common factor. Then if p/q is a rational root p divides an and q divides a0.



Proof:

Let p/q be a root..then f(p/q)=0

That is

ao(p/q)^n + a1(p/q)^n-1 +...+an=0

Or -p (a0p^n-1 + ... + an-1q^n-1)= anq^n

And aop^n = -q(a1p^n-1 +...+anq^n-1)

By this we know that p|an are coprime and q|a0.

topics.title: k 0=3, and I'm not trolling
topics.text:
So... I came across some people who claimed they proved $0=3$...

And they're not wrong (?)

Here's the proof.

Let $x(x+1)=-1$

$x^2+x=-1$

$x^2+x+1=0$

$x+1=-x^2$ (Keep this is mind. This isn't the next step)

Divide $x^2+x+1$ by $x$

$x+1+1/x=0$

$(x+1)+1/x=0$

$-x^2+1/x=0$

$x^2=1/x$

$x^3=1$

$x=1$

Substitute back $1$ to the original equation

$1(1+1)=-1$

$2=-1$

$3=0$

What the heck is going on?

On a side note, if we actually try to solve this equation the correct way...

$x^2+x+1=0$

$(x+1/2)^2=-3/4$

$x = -\frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot i$

If you plug both of them in the equation, you get

$$(-\frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot i)^2 + (- \frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot i ) + 1$$$$\frac{1}{4} \mp \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot i - \frac{3}{4} \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot i + \frac{1}{2}$$(the $\mp$ means that if we choose a sign in $\pm$ we take the opposite sign for the $\mp$, so $\pm x \mp x = 0$ for all $x$) $$\frac{1}{4} \mp \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot i - \frac{3}{4} \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot i + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{-1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 0,$$which is what we wanted.

Question has been resolved. Please refrain from posting unless necessary.
